peloneustes:enwiki:6.title: Peloneustes (Formerly assigned species and specimens, part 2)

facts.statement: Peloneustes philarchus has been synonymized with Plesiosaurus philarchus, Thaumatosaurus philarchus, Pliosaurus philarchus, and Peloneustes philarchus var. spathyrhynchus.
facts.quote: Plesiosaurus philarchus Seeley, 1869 Thaumatosaurus philarchus (Lydekker, 1888) Pliosaurus philarchus (Seeley, 1892) Peloneustes philarchus var. spathyrhynchus Linder, 1913

facts.statement: The genus Peloneustes was established by Richard Lydekker in 1889.
facts.quote: parent_authority: Lydekker, 1889

facts.statement: The species Peloneustes philarchus was first described by Harry Govier Seeley in 1869.
facts.quote: authority: (Seeley, 1869)

facts.statement: Peloneustes lived during the Middle Jurassic period.
facts.quote: Middle Jurassic

facts.statement: Peloneustes fossils are found in the Peterborough Member of the Oxford Clay Formation, dating to the Callovian age.
facts.quote: Peterborough Member of the Oxford Clay Formation, which is Callovian in age

facts.statement: The name Peloneustes means 'mud swimmer'.
facts.quote: Peloneustes (meaning mud swimmer)

facts.statement: Peloneustes reached a total length of 3.5 to 4 meters.
facts.quote: With a total length of 3.5 – 4 m, Peloneustes is not a large pliosaurid

facts.statement: Peloneustes had a large, triangular skull that made up about one-fifth of its body length.
facts.quote: It had a large, triangular skull, which occupied about a fifth of its body length

facts.statement: The front of the Peloneustes skull is elongated into a narrow snout.
facts.quote: The front of the skull is elongated into a narrow rostrum (snout)

facts.statement: Peloneustes had conical teeth with circular cross-sections and vertical ridges on all sides.
facts.quote: The teeth of Peloneustes are conical and have circular cross-sections, bearing vertical ridges on all sides

facts.statement: Peloneustes had a short neck consisting of only 19 to 21 cervical vertebrae.
facts.quote: With only 19 to 21 cervical (neck) vertebrae, Peloneustes had a short neck for a plesiosaur

facts.statement: Peloneustes had flipper-like limbs, with the rear pair being larger than the front pair.
facts.quote: The limbs of Peloneustes were modified into flippers, with the back pair larger than the front

facts.statement: Peloneustes lived in an epicontinental sea approximately 30 to 50 meters deep.
facts.quote: Peloneustes would have inhabited an epicontinental (inland) sea that was around 30 – 50 m deep

facts.statement: Peloneustes likely used its long, narrow snout to quickly catch fish by piercing them with sharp teeth.
facts.quote: The long, narrow snout of Peloneustes could have been swung quickly through the water to catch fish, which it pierced with its numerous sharp teeth

facts.statement: The holotype of Peloneustes philarchus was discovered by geologist Henry Porter in a clay pit near Peterborough, England.
facts.quote: discovered by geologist Henry Porter in a clay pit close to Peterborough, England

facts.statement: In 1866, Adam Sedgwick bought the holotype specimen for the University of Cambridge's Woodwardian Museum.
facts.quote: In 1866, geologist Adam Sedgwick purchased the specimen for the University of Cambridge's Woodwardian Museum

facts.statement: Harry Govier Seeley described the holotype as Plesiosaurus philarchus in 1869.
facts.quote: Seeley described the specimen as a new species of the preexisting genus Plesiosaurus, Plesiosaurus philarchus, in 1869

facts.statement: The specific name 'philarchus' means 'power-loving', possibly referring to the animal's large, powerful skull.
facts.quote: The specific name means power-loving, possibly due to its large, powerful skull

facts.statement: Richard Lydekker identified a specimen as Plesiosaurus philarchus and published a description in 1889.
facts.quote: Lydekker identified this specimen as an individual of Plesiosaurus philarchus and published a description of it in 1889

facts.statement: Lydekker initially assigned the species to Thaumatosaurus in 1888 but later created the new genus Peloneustes in 1889.
facts.quote: He initially assigned it to Thaumatosaurus in 1888, but later decided that it was distinct enough to warrant its own genus, which he named Peloneustes in his 1889 publication

facts.statement: Harry Govier Seeley classified Peloneustes within the genus Pliosaurus in 1892.
facts.quote: Seeley, however, lumped Peloneustes into Pliosaurus in 1892

facts.statement: Seeley and Lydekker disagreed on the classification of P. philarchus, reflecting a scientific feud between them.
facts.quote: Seeley and Lydekker could not agree on which genus to classify P. philarchus in, representing part of a feud between the two scientists

facts.statement: Charles William Andrews described the skull anatomy of Peloneustes in 1895 using four partial skulls from the Leeds Collection.
facts.quote: In 1895, palaeontologist Charles William Andrews described the anatomy of the skull of Peloneustes based on four partial skulls in the Leeds Collection

facts.statement: Hermann Linder described multiple Peloneustes philarchus specimens in 1913 from collections in Germany.
facts.quote: In 1913, naturalist Hermann Linder described multiple specimens of Peloneustes philarchus housed in the Institut für Geowissenschaften, University of Tübingen and State Museum of Natural History Stuttgart, Germany

facts.statement: A specimen described by Linder had a damaged cranium but a mostly undamaged mandible.
facts.quote: Only the rear part of the cranium was in good condition, but the mandible was mostly undamaged

facts.statement: A well-preserved skull specimen (GPIT RE/3409) preserved a scleral ring, marking the fourth time such bones were reported in a plesiosaur.
facts.quote: Another of the specimens Linder described was a well-preserved skull (GPIT RE/3409), also from the University of Tübingen, preserving a scleral ring (the set of small bones that support the eye), only the fourth time these bones had been reported in a plesiosaur

facts.statement: It is debated whether Peloneustes is a close relative of Pliosaurus or a more basal pliosaurid within Thalassophonea, with the latter view having more support.
facts.quote: Peloneustes has been interpreted as both a close relative of Pliosaurus or as a more basal (early-diverging) pliosaurid within Thalassophonea, with the latter interpretation finding more support

facts.statement: Andrews described the anatomy of Peloneustes primarily using well-preserved skulls and an almost complete skeleton from the Leeds Collection.
facts.quote: The anatomy of the Peloneustes specimens was described in the second volume, based primarily on the well-preserved skulls NHMUK R2679 and NHMUK R3808 and NHMUK R3318, an almost complete skeleton.

facts.statement: A nearly complete Peloneustes skeleton (NHMUK R3318) was well enough preserved to be rearticulated and mounted for display, though missing pelvic and limb parts were reconstructed.
facts.quote: NHMUK R3318 was so well preserved that it could be rearticulated and mounted, although the missing parts of the pelvis and limbs had to be filled in.

facts.statement: In 1910, Andrews created the first skeletal mount of a pliosaurid, which provided crucial information about the group's overall anatomy.
facts.quote: Andrews had described this mount in 1910, remarking that it was the first skeletal mount of a pliosaurid, thus providing important information about the overall anatomy of the group.

facts.statement: Ketchum and Benson described the skull anatomy of Peloneustes in 2011 using new specimens like NHMUK R4058, a three-dimensionally preserved skull that clarified its shape.
facts.quote: In 2011, palaeontologists Hilary Ketchum and Roger Benson described the anatomy of the skull of Peloneustes. Since the previous anatomical studies of Andrews and Linder, more specimens had been found, including NHMUK R4058, a skull preserved in three dimensions, providing a better idea of the skull's shape.

facts.statement: Tarlo declared the species P. aequalis invalid in 1960 because it was based on upper limb bones, which are insufficient for distinguishing pliosaurid species.
facts.quote: In his 1960 review of pliosaurid taxonomy, Tarlo considered P. aequalis to be invalid, since it was based on propodials (upper limb bones), which cannot be used to differentiate different pliosaurid species.

facts.statement: Tarlo suggested that Peloneustes sterrodeirus actually belongs to the genus Pliosaurus, possibly as a synonym of P. brachydeirus.
facts.quote: He considered Peloneustes sterrodeirus to instead belong to Pliosaurus, possibly within P. brachydeirus.

facts.statement: Andrews assigned a large pliosaur skeleton to Peloneustes evansi in 1913, noting its mandible and vertebrae differed significantly from those of Peloneustes philarchus.
facts.quote: In 1913, Andrews assigned a partial skeleton of another large pliosaur found by Leeds to Peloneustes evansi, noting that while the mandible and vertebrae were similar to other Peloneustes evansi specimens, they were quite different from those of Peloneustes philarchus.

facts.statement: Tarlo synonymized Peloneustes evansi with Peloneustes philarchus in 1960 because their cervical vertebrae were identical except for size differences.
facts.quote: In his 1960 review of pliosaurids, Tarlo synonymised Peloneustes evansi with Peloneustes philarchus due to their cervical vertebrae being identical (save for a difference in size).

facts.statement: Ketchum and Benson argued in 2011 that Peloneustes evansi is a nomen dubium (indeterminate species) because its holotype lacks distinguishing features.
facts.quote: Hilary F. Ketchum and Roger B. J. Benson disagreed with this synonymy, and in 2011 considered that since the holotype of Peloneustes evansi is nondiagnostic (lacking distinguishing features), P. evansi is a nomen dubium and therefore an indeterminate pliosaurid.

facts.statement: Ernst Koken suggested in 1905 that Plesiosaurus kanzleri, found in northern Germany, might belong to Peloneustes based on vertebral morphology.
facts.quote: In 1905, palaeontologist Ernst Koken described another species of Plesiosaurus, P. kanzleri, from two Early Cretaceous dorsal vertebrae discovered in a clay pit near Gronau, northern Germany. He nevertheless suggested that this species might belong to Peloneustes, owing to the morphology of these vertebrae.

facts.statement: Recent studies concluded that Plesiosaurus kanzleri remains a nomen dubium because the fossil material lacks diagnostic characters for confident assignment.
facts.quote: They nevertheless emphasized that the material lacks a diagnostic combination of characters that would allow a confident taxonomic assignment, and P. kanzleri therefore remains a nomen dubium.

facts.statement: Tarlo synonymized the subspecies in 1960, noting that the wider mandibular symphysis in larger specimens is likely due to intraspecific variation rather than a separate taxon.
facts.quote: Tarlo considered it to be a synonym of Peloneustes philarchus in 1960, and the mandibular symphysis of Peloneustes is proportionately wider in larger specimens, making this trait more likely to be due to intraspecific variation (variation within species).

facts.statement: Novozhilov named Peloneustes irgisensis in 1948 based on a partial skeleton (PIN 426) that included a skull, vertebrae, a hind limb, and preserved stomach contents.
facts.quote: In 1948, palaeontologist Nestor Novozhilov named a new species of Peloneustes, P. irgisensis, based on PIN 426, a partial skeleton consisting of a large, incomplete skull, vertebrae, and a partial hind limb, with stomach contents preserved.

facts.statement: Novozhilov moved the species to a new genus in 1964, but later studies reassigned it to Pliosaurus, possibly as a synonym of P. rossicus.
facts.quote: In 1964 Novozhilov erected a new genus, Strongylokrotaphus, for this species, but further studies concurred with Tarlo and reassigned the species to Pliosaurus, possibly a synonym of Pliosaurus rossicus.

facts.statement: Recent studies consider Peloneustes irgisensis a nomen dubium but recommend a new description of the holotype despite its damaged condition.
facts.quote: More recent studies considered the taxon as a nomen dubium given its currently undiagnostic character, but nevertheless recommend a new description of the holotype.

facts.statement: A new description of the holotype is difficult because the skull and mandible of specimen PIN 426 have been seriously damaged by pyrite decay and associated elements are lost.
facts.quote: However, this suggestion risks being tainted by the current state of conservation of specimen PIN 426, the skull and notably the mandible having since been seriously damaged by pyrite decay, and the associated elements being noted as lost.

facts.statement: Ketchum and Benson concluded in 2011 that the genus Peloneustes contains only one valid species, P. philarchus.
facts.quote: In 2011, Ketchum and Benson considered Peloneustes to contain only one species, P. philarchus.

facts.statement: Ketchum and Benson identified twenty-one definite specimens of Peloneustes philarchus, all originating from the Peterborough Member of the Oxford Clay Formation.
facts.quote: They recognised twenty one definite specimens of Peloneustes philarchus, all from the Peterborough Member of the Oxford Clay Formation.

facts.statement: Ketchum and Benson suggested that specimens from the Peterborough Member and Marquise, France, previously assigned to Peloneustes actually belong to unnamed pliosaurid species.
facts.quote: They considered some specimens from the Peterborough Member and Marquise, France previously assigned to Peloneustes to belong to different, currently unnamed pliosaurids.

facts.statement: Peloneustes is classified as a small to medium-sized pliosaurid.
facts.quote: Peloneustes is a small- to medium-sized member of Pliosauridae.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen GPIT-RE-3182 is estimated to have reached a body length of approximately 4.34 meters and a mass of around 1 metric ton.
facts.quote: This latter, numbered as GPIT-RE-3182, would have reached an estimated body length of approximately 4.34 m during its lifetime, for a body mass of around 1 MT.

facts.statement: Peloneustes belongs to the pliosauromorph morphotype, characterized by a large head where the skull makes up less than one-fifth of the total body length.
facts.quote: Peloneustes is of the latter morphotype, with its skull making up a little less than a fifth of the animal's total length.

facts.statement: Like other plesiosaurs, Peloneustes possessed a short tail, a massive torso, and limbs modified into large flippers.
facts.quote: Peloneustes, like all plesiosaurs, had a short tail, massive torso, and all of its limbs modified into large flippers.

facts.statement: The crania of Peloneustes vary in length between 60 and 78.5 centimeters.
facts.quote: These crania vary in size, measuring 60 - 78.5 cm in length.

facts.statement: Peloneustes possessed scleral rings made of at least 16 individual elements, which is an unusually high number for reptiles.
facts.quote: The scleral rings are composed of at least 16 individual elements, an unusually high number for a reptile.

facts.statement: Peloneustes is distinguished by a long cultriform process on the parasphenoid bone, visible when viewing the palate from below.
facts.quote: The parasphenoid (a bone that forms the lower front part of the braincase) bears a long cultriform process (a frontwards projection of the braincase) that is visible when the palate is viewed from below, another distinctive characteristic of Peloneustes.

facts.statement: Peloneustes has a unique elevated ridge on the mandibular symphysis where the dentaries meet, a feature not found in other plesiosaurs.
facts.quote: Between the tooth rows, the mandibular symphysis bears an elevated ridge where the dentaries meet. This is a unique feature of Peloneustes, not seen in any other plesiosaurs.

facts.statement: The teeth of Peloneustes have circular cross-sections, a trait shared with other pliosaurids of its time.
facts.quote: The teeth of Peloneustes have circular cross sections, as seen in other pliosaurids of its age.

facts.statement: Peloneustes had heterodont dentition, meaning it possessed teeth of different shapes.
facts.quote: The dentition of Peloneustes is heterodont, that is, it has teeth of different shapes.

facts.statement: Peloneustes had larger caniniform teeth at the front of its jaws and smaller, sharply recurved, stouter teeth further back.
facts.quote: The larger teeth are caniniform and located at the front of the jaws, while the smaller teeth are more sharply recurved, stouter, and located further back.

facts.statement: Andrews reported in 1913 that Peloneustes possessed 21 to 22 cervical, 2 to 3 pectoral, and approximately 20 dorsal vertebrae based on specimens from the Leeds Collection.
facts.quote: In 1913, Andrews reported that Peloneustes had 21 to 22 cervical, 2 to 3 pectoral, and around 20 dorsal vertebrae, with the exact number of sacral (hip) and caudal vertebrae unknown, based on specimens in the Leeds Collection.

facts.statement: In adult Peloneustes, the first two cervical vertebrae (atlas and axis) are fused, whereas in juveniles they exist as separate unfused elements.
facts.quote: The first two cervical vertebrae, the atlas and axis, are fused in adults, but in juveniles they are present as several unfused elements.

facts.statement: The cervical vertebrae of Peloneustes feature tall neural spines that are compressed laterally.
facts.quote: The cervical vertebrae bear tall neural spines that are compressed from side to side.

facts.statement: Each cervical centrum in Peloneustes possesses a strong keel running along the midline of its underside.
facts.quote: Each cervical centrum has a strong keel along the midline of its underside.

facts.statement: Peloneustes had a large shoulder girdle that was not as heavily constructed as in some other plesiosaur species.
facts.quote: The shoulder girdle of Peloneustes was large, although not as heavily built as in some other plesiosaurs.

facts.statement: The shoulder joint in Peloneustes is formed by the scapula and coracoid bones meeting at a 70-degree angle.
facts.quote: The shoulder joint is formed by both the scapula (shoulder balde) and the coracoid, with the two bones forming a 70° angle with each other.

facts.statement: The scapulae of Peloneustes are triradiate, bearing three prominent projections typical of pliosaurids.
facts.quote: The scapulae are typical in form for a pliosaurid and triradiate, bearing three prominent projections, or rami.

facts.statement: Peloneustes had hind limbs longer than its forelimbs, with the femur longer than the humerus, though the humerus was more robust.
facts.quote: The hind limbs of Peloneustes are longer than its forelimbs, with the femur being longer than the humerus, although the humerus is the more robust of the two elements.

facts.statement: The metacarpals, metatarsals, and proximal manual phalanges of Peloneustes are flattened.
facts.quote: The metacarpals, metatarsals, and the proximal manual phalanges (some of the bones making up the outer part of the paddle) are flattened.

facts.statement: Seeley initially described Peloneustes as a species of Plesiosaurus, a common practice at the time when genus scopes were similar to modern family definitions.
facts.quote: Seeley initially described Peloneustes as a species of Plesiosaurus, a rather common practice (at the time, the scope of genera was similar to what is currently used for families).

facts.statement: Lydekker placed Peloneustes in the family Pliosauridae in 1890, and it has remained consistently assigned to this family since.
facts.quote: In 1890, Lydekker placed Peloneustes in this family, to which it has been consistently assigned since.

facts.statement: O'Keefe recovered Peloneustes as a basal member of Pliosauridae in 2001, placing it outside a group containing Liopleurodon, Pliosaurus, and Brachauchenius.
facts.quote: In 2001, O'Keefe recovered it as a basal (early-diverging) member of this family, outside of a group including Liopleurodon, Pliosaurus, and Brachauchenius.

facts.statement: Smith and Dyke found in 2008 that Peloneustes is the sister taxon of Pliosaurus.
facts.quote: In 2008, palaeontologists Adam S. Smith and Gareth J. Dyke found Peloneustes to be the sister taxon of Pliosaurus.

facts.statement: Benson and Druckenmiller named the clade Thalassophonea in 2013, which included short-necked pliosaurids, and found Peloneustes to be the most basal member of this group.
facts.quote: In 2013, Benson and palaeontologist Patrick S. Druckenmiller named a new clade within Pliosauridae, Thalassophonea. This clade included the "classic", short-necked pliosaurids while excluding the earlier, long-necked, more gracile forms. Peloneustes was found to be the most basal thalassophonean.

facts.statement: The exact relationship between pliosaurids and other plesiosaurs remains uncertain.
facts.quote: Exactly how pliosaurids are related to other plesiosaurs is uncertain.

facts.statement: Samuel P. Welles argued in 1943 that pliosaurids were more similar to Polycotylidae due to shared characteristics like large skulls and short necks.
facts.quote: However, in 1943, palaeontologist Samuel P. Welles thought that pliosaurids were more similar to Polycotylidae, as they both had large skulls and short necks, among other characteristics.

facts.statement: Benson and colleagues recovered a different phylogenetic topology in 2012, suggesting Pliosauridae is more closely related to Plesiosauroidea than Rhomaleosauridae.
facts.quote: In 2012, Benson and colleagues recovered a different topology, with Pliosauridae being more closely related to Plesiosauroidea than Rhomaleosauridae.

facts.statement: Tarlo considered Peloneustes a close relative of Pliosaurus in 1960 because both shared elongated mandibular symphyses.
facts.quote: In 1960, Tarlo considered Peloneustes to be a close relative of Pliosaurus, since both taxa had elongated mandibular symphyses.

facts.statement: Peloneustes likely had a high metabolism and was either homeothermic or endothermic, growing at rates similar to birds.
facts.quote: Plesiosaurs were well-adapted to marine life. They grew at rates comparable to those of birds and had high metabolisms, indicating homeothermy or even endothermy.

facts.statement: The bony labyrinth in the skull of Peloneustes, which housed the balance and orientation organ, was shaped similarly to that of sea turtles.
facts.quote: The bony labyrinth, a hollow within the skull which held a sensory organ associated with balance and orientation, of Peloneustes and other plesiosaurs is similar in shape to that of sea turtles.

facts.statement: In 2017, James Neenan and colleagues hypothesized that the shape of the Peloneustes bony labyrinth evolved alongside the flapping swimming motions used by plesiosaurs.
facts.quote: Palaeontologist James Neenan and colleagues hypothesised in 2017 that this shape probably evolved alongside the flapping motions used by plesiosaurs to swim.

facts.statement: Peloneustes likely possessed salt glands in its head to manage excess salt in its body.
facts.quote: Peloneustes probably had salt glands in its head to cope with excess amount of salt within its body.

facts.statement: Because Peloneustes preyed on salt-poor vertebrates, Leslie Noè suggested in 2001 that its salt glands did not need to be especially large.
facts.quote: However, Peloneustes appears to have been a predator of vertebrates, which contain less salt than invertebrates, therefore leading palaeontologist Leslie Noè to suggest in a 2001 dissertation that these glands would not have had to be especially large.

facts.statement: Peloneustes exhibited a reduced level of bone ossification, a trait shared with many other pliosaurs.
facts.quote: Peloneustes, like many other pliosaurs, displayed a reduced level of ossification of its bones.

facts.statement: In 1996, Arthur Cruickshank and colleagues proposed that the reduced bone ossification in Peloneustes helped with buoyancy or maneuverability.
facts.quote: Palaeontologist Arthur Cruickshank and colleagues in 1996 proposed that this may have helped Peloneustes maintain its buoyancy or improved its manoeuvrability.

facts.statement: A 2019 study by Corinna Fleischle and colleagues found that Peloneustes had enlarged red blood cells that likely aided it while diving.
facts.quote: A 2019 study by palaeontologist Corinna Fleischle and colleagues found that plesiosaurs had enlarged red blood cells, based on the morphology of their vascular canals, which would have aided them while diving.

facts.statement: Peloneustes swam using a method called subaqueous flight, utilizing its flippers as hydrofoils.
facts.quote: Plesiosaurs such as Peloneustes employed a method of swimming known as subaqueous flight, using their flippers as hydrofoils.

facts.statement: Peloneustes was unusual among marine reptiles for using all four limbs for propulsion without moving its vertebral column.
facts.quote: Plesiosaurs are unusual among marine reptiles in that they used all four of their limbs, but not movements of the vertebral column, for propulsion.

facts.statement: The front flippers of Peloneustes had an aspect ratio of 6.36, while the rear flippers had an aspect ratio of 8.32.
facts.quote: The front flippers of Peloneustes have aspect ratios of 6.36, while the rear flippers have aspect ratios of 8.32.

facts.statement: The aspect ratios of Peloneustes' flippers were similar to the wing ratios of modern falcons.
facts.quote: These ratios are similar to those of the wings of modern falcons.

facts.statement: In 2001, O'Keefe proposed that Peloneustes could move quickly and nimbly to capture prey, though this movement was likely inefficient.
facts.quote: In 2001, O'Keefe proposed that, much like falcons, pliosauromorph plesiosaurs such as Peloneustes probably were capable of moving quickly and nimbly, albeit inefficiently, to capture prey.

facts.statement: In 2022, Susana Gutarra and colleagues found via computer modeling that Peloneustes produced more drag than similarly sized cetaceans or ichthyosaurs due to its large flippers.
facts.quote: Computer modelling by palaeontologist Susana Gutarra and colleagues in 2022 found that due to their large flippers, a plesiosaur would have produced more drag than a comparably-sized cetacean or ichthyosaur.

facts.statement: In 1988, Judy Massare proposed that Peloneustes could actively pursue food rather than waiting, thanks to its shorter, deeper body reducing drag.
facts.quote: Due to the reduction in drag by their shorter, deeper bodies, palaeontologist Judy Massare proposed in 1988 that plesiosaurs could actively search for and pursue their food instead of having to lie in wait for it.

facts.statement: To prevent damage during feeding, the skull of Peloneustes was highly akinetic, with the cranium and mandible largely locked in place.
facts.quote: To avoid damage while feeding, the skulls of pliosaurids like Peloneustes are highly akinetic, where the bones of the cranium and mandible were largely locked in place to prevent movement.

facts.statement: Peloneustes had an enlarged coronoid eminence for jaw muscle anchorage, though it was smaller than in other contemporary pliosaurids.
facts.quote: The enlarged coronoid eminence provides a large, strong region for the anchorage of the jaw muscles, although this structure is not as large in Peloneustes as it is in other contemporary pliosaurids.

facts.statement: The numerous teeth of Peloneustes were rarely broken but frequently showed wear at their tips.
facts.quote: The numerous teeth of Peloneustes rarely are broken, but often show signs of wear at their tips.

facts.statement: The sharp, slightly curved, gracile shape and prominent spacing of Peloneustes' teeth indicate they were built for piercing.
facts.quote: Their sharp points, slightly curved, gracile shape, and prominent spacing indicate that they were built for piercing.

facts.statement: Based on its snout and tooth morphology, Leslie Noè suggested that Peloneustes was a piscivore.
facts.quote: Both the snout and tooth morphologies led Noè to suggest that Peloneustes was a piscivore (fish eater).

facts.statement: Peloneustes likely caught prey by quickly swinging its head to the side, using its drag-minimizing snout and long jaws to snap up mobile prey.
facts.quote: Peloneustes would have quickly swung its head to the side. The gracile snout's roughly circular cross-section would have minimized drag, while the long jaws were suited for quickly snapping up mobile prey.

facts.statement: Because the snout tip was far from the jaw joint, Peloneustes exerted a weaker bite force at the front than at the back.
facts.quote: Since the tip of the snout was further away from the jaw joint, it would have exerted a weaker bite force than the regions further back.

facts.statement: Peloneustes' adaptations indicate a preference for smaller, agile prey that was easier to incapacitate.
facts.quote: These adaptations indicate a preference for smaller prey that, while agile, would have been easier to incapacitate and less powerful.

facts.statement: Despite its adaptations, Peloneustes was still capable of attacking fish of moderate size.
facts.quote: However, Peloneustes would still have been capable of attacking fish of moderate size.

facts.statement: A skeleton (NHMUK R3317) with belemnite remains assigned to Peloneustes by Andrews in 1910 is incomplete and may actually belong to Simolestes, as suggested by Noè.
facts.quote: While a skeleton, catalogued as NHMUK R3317, with belemnite remains in its stomach was assigned to Peloneustes by Andrews in 1910, it is very incomplete and may actually belong to the contemporaneous pliosaurid Simolestes instead, as suggested by Noè.

facts.statement: In 2018, Bruce Rothschild and colleagues suggested that Peloneustes inflicted bite marks on a Cryptoclidus specimen.
facts.quote: Peloneustes has also been suggested to have inflicted bite marks upon a specimen of Cryptoclidus by Bruce Rothschild and colleagues in 2018.

facts.statement: Peloneustes fossils are known from the Peterborough Member of the Oxford Clay Formation.
facts.quote: Peloneustes is known from the Peterborough Member (formerly known as the Lower Oxford Clay) of the Oxford Clay Formation.

facts.statement: Although sometimes listed as Oxfordian, the Peterborough Member where Peloneustes is found dates to the Callovian stage of the Middle Jurassic.
facts.quote: While Peloneustes has been listed as coming from the Oxfordian stage (spanning from about to million years ago) of the Upper Jurassic, the Peterborough Member actually dates to the Callovian stage (spanning from about to million years ago) of the Middle Jurassic.

facts.statement: The Peterborough Member spans from the late lower to early upper Callovian, covering the entirety of the Middle Callovian.
facts.quote: The Peterborough Member spans from the late lower Callovian to the early upper Callovian, occupying the entirety of the Middle Callovian.

facts.statement: The Peterborough Member is about 16 to 25 meters thick and stretches from Dorset to the Humber.
facts.quote: The member is about 16 - 25 m thick, stretching from Dorset to the Humber.

facts.statement: When deposited, the environment of Peloneustes was located at a latitude of 35°N.
facts.quote: When it was deposited, it would have been located at a latitude of 35°N.

facts.statement: The Oxford Clay sea, where Peloneustes lived, was largely encircled by islands and continents that provided sediment.
facts.quote: This sea, known as the Oxford Clay sea, was largely encircled by islands and continents, which provided the seaway with sediment.

facts.statement: The Oxford Clay Sea connected the Tethys Ocean to the south and boreal regions to the north, allowing faunal interchange.
facts.quote: The southern region of the Oxford Clay Sea was connected to the Tethys Ocean, while it was connected to more boreal regions on its northern side.

facts.statement: The sea where Peloneustes lived was approximately 30 to 50 meters deep within 150 kilometers of the shoreline.
facts.quote: This sea was approximately 30 - 50 m deep within 150 km of the shoreline.

facts.statement: Based on bivalve isotopes, the seabed water temperature where Peloneustes lived varied from 14 to 17°C seasonally, averaging 15°C.
